The group moved to the courtroom. Lin Xiugu was brought in, weeping as she recounted her grievances. No sooner had Wang Youcai heard her out than he struck the gavel, ready to pass judgment. At that moment, Jiang Rao let out a soft "Ah."

The sound was not loud, but it was enough for everyone in the hall to hear. Wang Youcai frowned at her. "What is it, Madam?"

Jiang Rao seemed startled, shrinking back toward Qianlong and whispering, "I... I just find it strange." She raised her eyes, looking timidly at Wang Youcai. "This woman says she has a land deed as proof; why does the Magistrate not look at it? Though I do not understand the law, I know that one must rely on evidence to judge a case."

She spoke with such innocent naivety, and paired with her beautiful face, anyone would have thought she was merely asking a simple question. But to Wang Youcai, every word was a prick to his conscience.

"I have my own ways of judging cases," Wang Youcai said, his face darkening.

"Oh..." Jiang Rao lowered her head, twisting her handkerchief, but muttered in a voice loud enough to be heard, "But I’ve heard that when a righteous official judges a case, they always look at the evidence... Could it be that there is something wrong with this evidence?"

Her "muttering" was perfectly timed; the onlookers outside the hall heard it clearly, and whispers immediately began to spread.

Wang Youcai’s face turned livid. Just as he was about to lash out, Qianlong stood up and walked into the center of the hall, taking the petition from Lin Xiugu’s hands. "Since Magistrate Wang will not look at it, I shall look at it for you."

"Audacious!" Wang Youcai slammed his gavel and rose. "How dare you act so presumptuously in a court of law!"

Qianlong ignored him. After reading the petition, he raised his eyes and said coldly, "Wang Youcai, as a local official, you have been corrupt and lawless, shielding your relatives. What say you to these crimes?"

"You—" Before Wang Youcai could finish, Ji Xiaolan revealed his imperial token. "Ji Yun, attendant before the throne, is here! The Emperor has arrived; why do you not kneel and welcome him!"

The entire hall fell into a deathly silence.

Wang Youcai looked at Qianlong—the man who had just appeared to be a mere merchant now stood with his hands behind his back, his eyes filled with imperial majesty. His legs went weak, and he collapsed to the floor with a thud.

Beside him, Jiang Rao let out a soft sigh of relief and patted her chest. "That was finally over; I was nervous to death."

Her delicate and naive demeanor stood in stark contrast to the grim atmosphere of the courtroom. Yet, it was she who, with just a few words, had become the final straw that broke Wang Youcai.

Qianlong looked back at her, a hint of a smile flashing in his eyes. Jiang Rao gave him a secret wink, then immediately resumed the dignified air of "Madam Ai."

Ji Xiaolan witnessed this scene, and the old official stroked his beard and smiled to himself, thinking: This Consort Chen is truly full of surprises.

And from this moment on, the sky over Qinghe Town was truly about to change.

chapters.title: The Lotus Boat Disturbance
chapters.content:
After Qianlong finished dealing with the case of Wang Youcai, he remained in Qinghe Town for one more day. Ji Xiaolan and the others were busy handling the aftermath, inventorying Liu Fugui’s assets to return them to the people, and arranging for a new magistrate. Qianlong, meanwhile, took Jiang Rao and the others on a stroll through the town in plain clothes to observe the changes in the lives of the people.

Qinghe Town had indeed changed. The streets were bustling, smiles had returned to the faces of the commoners, and even the storyteller in the teahouse was recounting the tale of "The Emperor’s Incognito Visit and Wise Punishment of the Corrupt Official." Although the details had been exaggerated and dramatized, the longing for clean and honest governance was genuine.

That evening, as the group dined at the inn, Ji Xiaolan reported that the new magistrate would arrive the next day—a young official known for his integrity. Qianlong nodded. "Tell him to govern well. I will keep an eye on this place after I return to the capital."

The next morning, the caravan prepared to leave Qinghe Town. The townspeople gathered early at the entrance to see them off, kneeling in rows. Qianlong did not linger; he simply lifted the carriage curtain, nodded to the people, and ordered the caravan to depart.

As the carriage pulled onto the main road, the autumn sun was just right. Jiang Rao leaned against Qianlong’s shoulder, toying with the white jade hairpin in her hand, and suddenly asked, "Your Majesty, we have been out for quite some time; won’t the palace be worried?"

"Li Yu will handle it," Qianlong said, closing his eyes to rest.

Jiang Rao said "Oh" and fell silent, watching the scenery fly by outside the window. About an hour later, a vast expanse of water appeared ahead—a fairly large lake. It being autumn, the lotus leaves in the lake were withered, though a few scattered seed pods still stood tall. Several small boats wove across the water as lotus pickers harvested the last of the autumn crop.

"Stop and let us rest a while," Qianlong ordered.

The caravan stopped by the lake. Everyone stepped out to stretch their limbs. The lake water was clear, and the autumn breeze blew by, carrying a cool, watery chill. Little Swallow was the most energetic; she grabbed Yongqi and ran toward the lake. "Look, Yongqi! There are boats over there! Shall we go pick some lotus pods?"

Yongqi shook his head with a smile. "The pods are all old this time of year; there’s no use picking them."

"It’s just for fun!" Little Swallow insisted. "I’ve never picked lotus pods before!"

As they were talking, a soft sobbing sound came from the lakeside. The group followed the sound and saw a young girl in plain clothes kneeling under a tree by the lake. In front of her lay a piece of coarse cloth with the words "Selling Myself to Bury My Father" written on it. The girl was about sixteen or seventeen, with delicate features; she was currently teary-eyed and pitiful.

Little Swallow was the first to rush over. "Miss, what’s wrong?"

The girl looked up. Seeing Little Swallow’s fine clothes and the group of distinguished-looking people behind her, hope ignited in her eyes. "Miss, I am a lotus picker from the village by the lake. My father passed away yesterday from illness, and I have no money for his burial, so I have no choice but to sell myself here..." As she spoke, she covered her face and sobbed again.

Little Swallow felt a pang of sympathy and turned to look at Yongqi. Yongqi understood and stepped forward, saying gently, "How much silver do you need to bury your father?"

The lotus picker raised her tearful eyes, and upon seeing Yongqi’s handsome and noble appearance, her face flushed slightly. "Ten... ten taels of silver would be enough."

Yongqi took out the silver and handed it to her. "Go quickly and see to the funeral."

The lotus picker took the silver but did not leave. Instead, she kowtowed and said, "Young Master, your kindness is great. Since I have already offered to sell myself, I am now your person. Please, Young Master, take me in..."

"There is no need," Yongqi said quickly. "This silver is a gift; there is no need to sell yourself."

"How can that be?" the lotus picker insisted. "My father taught me that one must be grateful for kindness. Since I have written the contract of sale, I must keep my word."

The two went back and forth—one insisting on repaying the kindness, the other firmly refusing to accept. Little Swallow watched from the side. At first, she felt sorry for the girl, but as she watched, she gradually felt that something was off—why was this lotus picker looking at Yongqi with such... such clingy eyes?

She frowned, staring at the lotus picker’s tear-streaked face, then at Yongqi’s gentle and patient expression, and a nameless fire suddenly flared in her heart.

Jiang Rao watched this scene from not far away, the corners of her mouth curling up involuntarily. She nudged Qianlong with her elbow and whispered, "Your Majesty, look."

Qianlong followed her gaze and saw Little Swallow with her face taut, her eyes wide and round, staring at Yongqi and the lotus picker. She looked exactly like a small animal guarding its food.

"What’s wrong with Little Swallow?" Qianlong asked, puzzled. "Why is her expression so sour?"

Jiang Rao pursed her lips and smiled, a cunning light in her eyes. "Can’t Your Majesty tell?"

"Tell what?" Qianlong was even more confused.

Jiang Rao leaned into his ear, lowered her voice, and said with a smile, "Little Swallow is... unhappy."

"Unhappy?" Qianlong looked at Little Swallow. He saw that she was indeed displeased, but he still didn't understand. "Why is she unhappy? Yongqi is doing a good deed; she should be happy."

*My god!* Jiang Rao almost laughed out loud. How could this Emperor, so wise and martial in state affairs, be so dense in matters like this? Little Swallow was clearly jealous—jealous of that lotus picker girl! Yet the Emperor was still taking it seriously as a good deed!

She suppressed her laughter and said mysteriously, "Think about it, Your Majesty. Little Swallow is usually the most lively; she should be clapping and cheering to see Yongqi helping someone. But look at her now—her mouth is pouting enough to hang an oil bottle, and she’s glaring at that lotus picker girl as if she wants to burn a hole through her. Does that look like she’s happy?"

Qianlong looked carefully and indeed saw Little Swallow glaring "ferociously" at the lotus picker, while Yongqi was still patiently trying to persuade her to take back the contract, completely oblivious to Little Swallow’s odd behavior.

"This girl..." Qianlong chuckled. "Yongqi is helping her, and she’s the one who’s unhappy. She really has a child’s temper."

*A child’s temper?!* Jiang Rao laughed wildly in her heart. *Your Majesty, you really are... a straight-man thinker! This isn’t a child’s temper; this is a young girl’s heart! But then again, in your eyes, Little Swallow is your daughter. If a daughter is bickering with her 'brother,' of course you’d think it’s a child’s temper.*

The more she thought about it, the funnier it became. She couldn't help but cover her mouth with her handkerchief, her shoulders shaking slightly.

Seeing her laughing so strangely, Qianlong asked, "What are you laughing at again?"

"It’s nothing," Jiang Rao blinked, looking innocent. "I just think... Little Swallow looks quite cute like this."

Qianlong looked at the pouting Little Swallow, then at Jiang Rao, who was smiling like a little fox, and shook his head. "You women, your thoughts are truly hard to understand."

Over there, Yongqi finally convinced the lotus picker to go back and bury her father. The lotus picker left, looking back every few steps, and the resentful look she gave before leaving only made Little Swallow even angrier.

"Hmph!" Little Swallow tossed her head and turned to walk toward the carriage.

"Little Swallow?" Yongqi hurried to catch up. "What’s wrong?"

"Nothing’s wrong!" Little Swallow didn't stop.

"Then why are you angry?"

"Who’s angry? I’m not angry!"

The two walked and chased, their voices fading into the distance.

Jiang Rao watched their retreating figures and finally couldn't help but laugh out loud. Qianlong watched her laughing until she was trembling and said helplessly, "You, you just love to watch the drama."

"Isn't this drama wonderful?" Jiang Rao wiped away the tears of laughter. "Don't you think so, Your Majesty? The Fifth Prince is such a smart person, yet he’s so foolish at a time like this."

Qianlong laughed too. "Yongqi is simple-hearted. He only sees that the girl is pitiful; he doesn't think about anything else." As he spoke, he suddenly looked at Jiang Rao, his eyes deep. "And what about you? How much of your heart can I understand?"

Jiang Rao was startled, then pushed him away with a coquettish pout. "Your Majesty is teasing me again."

Qianlong took her hand, smiled, and said nothing.

The convoy set off again. Inside the carriage shared by Xiaoyanzi and Yongqi, the atmosphere was somewhat subtle. Xiaoyanzi sat in the corner, arms crossed, looking out the window and ignoring Yongqi. Yongqi sat opposite her, trying to speak several times, only to be glared back into silence.

The carriage jolted forward, leaving the autumn lake behind. The interlude with Miss Cailian was soon forgotten by most, save for Xiaoyanzi, who would occasionally mutter, "That Cailian, she didn't look like a good person at all," only to be coaxed back into a good mood by Yongqi’s gentle words.

In another carriage:

Jiang Rao turned to look at the Qianlong Emperor, who was resting with his eyes closed beside her. This man was the ruler of the nation, Ziwei’s biological father, Xiaoyanzi’s nominal father, and her own husband. He carried the weight of the empire on his shoulders, held the common people in his heart, and still had to deal with these tangled, messy threads of family and love...

Being an emperor is quite tiring, Jiang Rao thought, leaning gently against his shoulder.

Qianlong opened his eyes and pulled her closer. "Tired?"

"A little," Jiang Rao said, eyes closed. "And you, Your Majesty?"

"I am not tired," Qianlong said in a gentle voice. "With you by my side, I am not tired."

The corners of Jiang Rao’s mouth curled upward.

chapters.title: Strange Tales of Longfeng Town
chapters.content:
The convoy left the autumn lake and continued westward. On the road, Xiaoyanzi was still sulking about the Cailian incident. After much persuasion, Yongqi finally promised to buy her three skewers of candied haws to appease her. Hearing the commotion from the carriage ahead, Jiang Rao laughed until she couldn't straighten up.

Qianlong looked at her helplessly. "You, you just love watching such excitement."

"It's so interesting," Jiang Rao wiped away the tears of laughter. "Don't you think so, Your Majesty? The Fifth Prince is usually so steady, but in front of Xiaoyanzi, he’s like a completely different person."

Qianlong smiled as well. "That boy, Yongqi, truly dotes on Xiaoyanzi without limit." He paused, as if thinking of something, his tone softening. "But that is fine. That girl, Xiaoyanzi, suffered a lot while growing up outside; now that she has someone to cherish and spoil her, I am at ease."

Jiang Rao’s heart stirred. Qianlong spoke naturally; he clearly truly cherished Xiaoyanzi as a daughter. She felt a sudden sense of emotion—this man, the supreme ruler, was genuinely kind to his "daughter."

It’s a pity, she sighed inwardly, you’re doting on the wrong person. Your real daughter is sitting in the carriage behind.

But she could not say this, so she could only agree: "Xiaoyanzi is blessed. She has the Fifth Prince to cherish her, and you, her 'Imperial Father,' to spoil her."

Qianlong shook his head with a smile and said nothing more.

The convoy traveled for another half-day until a town appeared ahead. The stone tablet at the entrance was inscribed with the characters "Longfeng Town" in a rustic, vigorous hand. Looking from afar, the houses in the town were orderly, and the streets were bustling with people.

"The name of this town is quite interesting," Jiang Rao said, lifting the carriage curtain to look out. "Longfeng Chengxiang—a wonderful omen."

Ji Xiaolan reported from outside the carriage, "Your Majesty, Longfeng Town is famous for its 'Dragon and Phoenix Wells.' It is said that the two wells, one dragon and one phoenix, have sweet water that can cure a hundred illnesses. During temple fairs, people from a hundred miles around come to fetch the water."

"Oh?" Qianlong became interested. "Then let us go in and take a look."

The convoy entered the town. Indeed, Longfeng Town was more prosperous than the previous ones. Shops lined both sides of the street, mostly selling items related to dragons and phoenixes—dragon and phoenix jade pendants, embroidery featuring the auspicious pair, and even stalls selling "Dragon and Phoenix Well Water" in small jars, claimed to be able to ward off illness and disaster.

Xiaoyanzi had long since put the Cailian matter behind her, pulling Ziwei along to look at everything. "Ziwei, look! That dragon and phoenix jade pendant is so pretty! Let’s buy a pair, shall we? One for you and one for me!"

Yongqi laughed behind her, "You, you want to buy everything you see."

"It’s pretty!" Xiaoyanzi said righteously.

As they were browsing, the sound of gongs and drums suddenly erupted ahead. Everyone followed the sound and saw a high platform erected in the middle of the street. A middle-aged man stood on it, shouting, "Dear villagers! Today is our Longfeng Town’s triennial 'Treasure Hunt'! The old rules apply—whoever can solve these three riddles will receive my Li family’s ancestral 'Dragon and Phoenix Jade Disc'!"

A large crowd gathered below, discussing animatedly. Xiaoyanzi loved excitement and pulled everyone forward to squeeze in. "A treasure hunt? How fun! Let’s go see!"

Pushing to the front, they saw the man take out a jade disc from his robe. The disc was circular, pure white, and carved with a dragon and a phoenix, lifelike. Under the sunlight, the jade glowed with a warm luster; it was truly a fine object.

"Shopkeeper Li is showing off again!" an old man nearby shook his head. "Every three years, and every time, no one can solve his three riddles. I’m afraid this jade disc will never be given away."

"What kind of riddles are so hard?" Xiaoyanzi asked curiously.

The old man stroked his beard and said, "The Li family’s riddles are always bizarre. Last year it was, 'Four legs in the morning, two legs at noon, three legs in the evening,' guess the object. How is anyone supposed to guess that?"

Jiang Rao almost laughed out loud upon hearing this—wasn't this the famous Sphinx riddle? It had become an unsolvable mystery in this era.

On the platform, Shopkeeper Li began the first riddle: "Listen well! 'Has eyes but no pupils, has a mouth but no heart, has ears but cannot hear, has hands but no fingers.' Guess the object!"

The crowd below erupted. People guessed everything from "stone statue" to "puppet" to "clay figurine," but Shopkeeper Li only shook his head.

Xiaoyanzi scratched her head. "What is this? Has eyes but no pupils... is it a blind person?"

Yongqi laughed, "A blind person has a mouth and a heart, so it’s not 'has a mouth but no heart'."

Ziwei frowned in thought, and Erkang helped her ponder. Jiang Rao watched from the side, the answer clear as day—wasn't it a "painting"? The eyes in a painting have no pupils, the mouth doesn't speak, the ears don't hear, and the hands have no fingers.

But she didn't say anything. In such an occasion, it was better to keep a low profile.

Qianlong suddenly spoke: "Is it a painting?"

Shopkeeper Li was stunned and looked at Qianlong. "This gentleman guessed correctly! It is indeed a painting!" He was surprised. "What great wisdom, sir! No one has guessed this first riddle in three years!"

The crowd gasped in amazement. Everyone looked at Qianlong with admiration.

Qianlong smiled slightly, not taking the credit. "Just a lucky guess."

Jiang Rao tugged on his sleeve quietly and whispered, "Your Majesty is truly brilliant," her eyes full of smiles.

Qianlong pinched her hand and whispered, "You guessed it too, didn't you?"

Jiang Rao blinked, playing dumb. "I couldn't have guessed it."

Qianlong smiled without a word.

Shopkeeper Li cleared his throat. "Second riddle! 'Viewed from afar, the mountains have color; listened to up close, the water makes no sound. Flowers bloom even when spring departs; birds do not startle when people approach.' Guess the object!"

Once this riddle was out, the crowd became even quieter. The riddle was poetic and picturesque, yet even more baffling.

Xiaoyanzi muttered, "Viewed from afar, the mountains have color... mountains naturally have color. Listened to up close, the water makes no sound... how can water be silent?"

Ziwei said softly, "This seems to be describing... something that doesn't move?"

Jiang Rao laughed inwardly: Isn't this a "painting"? A landscape painting has color from afar, no sound of water up close; the flowers in the painting bloom all year round, and the birds don't fly away when people approach.

She looked at Qianlong, and Qianlong looked back at her, both sharing a knowing smile.

This time, Qianlong didn't rush to speak. After waiting a while and seeing that no one else could solve it, he said slowly, "Is it a painting?"

Shopkeeper Li’s eyes widened. "Again... correct!" He looked Qianlong up and down. "You are not a local, sir? Have you heard this riddle before?"

"Never," Qianlong shook his head. "Just a wild guess."

The crowd was already in an uproar. Solving two in a row could not be explained by luck.

Shopkeeper Li took a deep breath and brought out the final riddle: "Third riddle! This one is the hardest—'Green in youth, yellow in old age, hammered and beaten to form a pair. You see a friend off for a thousand miles, but eventually you must part; discarded by the roadside, leaving the old for the new.' Guess the object!"

When this riddle was posed, even Jiang Rao was stunned. The first two lines sounded like a plant, while the last two sounded like human affairs... what was this?

The crowd looked at each other, completely bewildered.

Qianlong also frowned in thought. Jiang Rao quietly tugged his sleeve and whispered, "Your Majesty, this one... I think I know."

Qianlong looked at her, surprise flashing in his eyes. "You know?"

Jiang Rao nodded and leaned into his ear, whispering two words. Qianlong was startled, then suddenly enlightened, a smile appearing in his eyes.

Seeing that no one could guess, Shopkeeper Li was about to speak when Qianlong said, "Is it... a straw sandal?"

The whole place went silent.

The jade disc in Shopkeeper Li’s hand almost fell to the ground. "H-how did you guess that, sir?"

Qianlong laughed, "Green in youth refers to the grass, yellow in old age refers to the dried grass. Hammered and beaten to weave a pair of shoes. You see a friend off for a thousand miles wearing straw sandals; when it is time to part, the worn-out sandals are discarded by the roadside—is that the logic?"

Shopkeeper Li nodded blankly, taking a long moment to recover before offering the jade disc with both hands. "Great talent, sir! This jade disc... it is yours!"

Thunderous applause erupted from the crowd. Everyone looked at Qianlong with admiration.

Qianlong took the jade disc but handed it to Jiang Rao. "You play with it."

Jiang Rao was stunned. "For me?"

"Yes," Qianlong smiled. "You helped me solve the last riddle, so it belongs to you."

Jiang Rao blushed and took the jade disc. The jade felt warm to the touch, and the dragon and phoenix carving was exquisite; it was truly a high-quality piece. She tucked it away carefully, and when she looked up at Qianlong, her eyes were full of smiles.

Shopkeeper Li said a few more words of praise before stepping down. The crowd gradually dispersed, and everyone continued to explore the town.

Xiaoyanzi was still immersed in the excitement. "That gentleman was so amazing! He guessed all three riddles! That Shopkeeper Li’s eyes were as big as copper bells!"

Yongqi laughed, "The gentleman is very learned; it’s no surprise he solved the riddles."

Ziwei said softly, "That last riddle was truly hard to guess. How did the gentleman think of straw sandals?"

Qianlong glanced at Jiang Rao, and she hurriedly lowered her head. Qianlong smiled, "Just a sudden flash of inspiration."

As everyone walked along chatting, Jiang Rao quietly tugged on Qianlong’s sleeve. When he leaned down, she whispered, "How did Your Majesty know it was me who guessed it?"

"Could that little look of yours hide anything from me?" Qianlong’s eyes held a smile. "When I mentioned 'straw sandals,' your eyes lit up."

Jiang Rao pursed her lips and smiled, feeling sweet inside.

When they reached the west end of the town, they indeed saw the "Dragon and Phoenix Wells." The two wells stood side-by-side, one carved with a dragon on the rim, the other with a phoenix. The water was clear, and many villagers were busy fetching it.

The person in charge of the wells was an old man with white hair. Seeing them approach, he greeted them with a smile: "Are you travelers from out of town? Would you like to taste the water from the Dragon and Phoenix Wells? The Dragon Well water is crisp and cool, while the Phoenix Well water is clear and sweet. When the water from both wells is mixed together, it becomes 'The Dragon and Phoenix Bringing Prosperity,' which is the most nourishing."

Xiaoyanzi was the most curious. "Really? Then I want to try it!"

The old man drew half a bucket of water from the Dragon Well and half from the Phoenix Well, mixed them together, scooped up a bowl, and handed it to Xiaoyanzi. After taking a sip, Xiaoyanzi’s eyes lit up. "It’s really good! It’s so clear and sweet!"

The others also tasted it, and it was indeed refreshing and delicious.

Qianlong asked the old man, "How old are these wells?"

"At least two or three hundred years," the old man said, stroking his beard. "According to my ancestors, they existed back in the previous dynasty. Strangely enough, Dragon and Phoenix Town has enjoyed favorable weather every year with no major disasters or calamities, and everyone says it is because of the protection of these wells."

Qianlong nodded and ordered his men to draw two buckets of water to take with them, saying it would be for the road.

It was already late when they left the Dragon and Phoenix Wells. They found an inn in town to stay for the night. During dinner, the innkeeper, having heard that they had solved the three riddles of the Li family, specially sent over a few signature dishes, saying it was to pay tribute to Qianlong’s wit.

Jiang Rao took out the Dragon and Phoenix jade pendant to admire it, liking it more the longer she looked. Qianlong watched from the side and laughed, "Are you this happy over just one jade pendant?"

"But this was won by the Emperor," Jiang Rao said, pressing the pendant against her cheek, her eyes curving into crescents. "The meaning is different."

Qianlong felt a stir in his heart and reached out to pull her into his arms. "Then I shall win more for you in the future."

"That’s a promise, then." Jiang Rao leaned into his embrace, playing with the pendant. "But next time there’s a riddle like that, let me show off a bit too. Just watching the Emperor be so impressive makes my hands itch."

Qianlong chuckled. "Very well, I'll let you do it next time."

The two chatted and laughed for a while longer before retiring for the night.

Deep in the night, Dragon and Phoenix Town grew quiet. Jiang Rao lay beside Qianlong, still holding the jade pendant in her hand, a smile on her lips.

Outside the window, the moonlight was like water, spilling onto the Dragon and Phoenix jade pendant. The dragon scales and phoenix feathers seemed to come alive, shimmering with a faint luster in the moonlight.

Jiang Rao closed her eyes and soon drifted into a dream. In her dream, she seemed to see the dragon and phoenix on the jade pendant actually take flight, circling and dancing around her, scattering a trail of auspiciousness.

***

### Chapter 40: This Moment is Perfect

During the few extra days they stayed in Dragon and Phoenix Town, the autumn rain fell intermittently, giving the small town a hazy, ethereal charm reminiscent of the Jiangnan water country. Qianlong’s health had greatly improved, so he decided to wait until the weather cleared completely before leaving.

On the afternoon of this day, the rain finally stopped, and the sky revealed a clear, limpid blue. Jiang Rao woke from her nap and pushed open the window; the humid air rushed in, carrying the unique freshness that follows rain. She took a deep breath, turned to Qianlong, who was reading, and said, "Your Majesty, the sky has cleared! Shall we go out for a walk?"

Qianlong put down his book. Seeing her eyes sparkling with anticipation, he smiled and asked, "Where would you like to go?"

"Just a casual stroll." Jiang Rao walked over to him and tugged gently on his sleeve. "There is a small river at the west end of town, and I heard there is a grove of osmanthus trees by the bank that should be in bloom these days. Shall we go see the osmanthus flowers?"

Her coquettish manner softened Qianlong’s heart. He put down his book and stood up. "Very well, let’s go see the osmanthus."

The two changed into casual clothes. Jiang Rao specifically chose a goose-yellow cheongsam covered by a pale cyan vest, with the white jade hairpin tucked into her hair, looking both elegant and charming. Qianlong wore an indigo long robe, with the mandarin duck-shaped pouch Jiang Rao had bought him tied at his waist—a pouch he now wore every day, which always made Jiang Rao’s eyes curve with joy whenever she saw it.

They left the inn and walked west along the bluestone path. The town after the rain was exceptionally tranquil; water still dripped from the eaves, splashing into tiny droplets on the stone slabs. Occasionally, children ran past, their laughter crisp and clear.

After walking for the time it takes to drink a cup of tea, they caught the faint scent of flowers. Turning a street corner, a grove of osmanthus trees came into view. It was the peak of the blooming season; golden osmanthus flowers were densely packed on the branches, their fragrance rich but not cloying, drifting on the breeze and refreshing the heart.

"It smells so good!" Jiang Rao let go of Qianlong’s hand and trotted into the grove. She spun around under a tree, looking up at the flowers covering the branches, her face filled with pure joy.

Qianlong followed behind her, watching her lively figure with a smile in his eyes. These past few days, she had finally regained her former liveliness and was no longer as polite and distant as she had been, which put his mind at ease.

"Your Majesty, look!" Jiang Rao suddenly pointed to a unique osmanthus tree. "This tree has silver osmanthus flowers!"

Qianlong walked over and indeed saw that the tree was covered in small, silvery-white flowers, which looked exceptionally elegant amidst the sea of gold. Jiang Rao stood on her tiptoes, wanting to pick a branch, but she wasn't tall enough; she jumped twice but still couldn't reach.

Qianlong shook his head with a smile, reached up, easily snapped off a branch, and handed it to her. "If you want it, just ask. Why jump?"

Jiang Rao took the flower branch and wrinkled her nose. "I wanted to pick it myself." She brought the branch to her nose and sniffed. "The silver osmanthus has a lighter scent, but it’s more refined." As she spoke, she tucked the branch into her hair and turned to ask Qianlong, "Does it look good?"

The goose-yellow outfit and the silvery-white flowers set off her skin, which was fairer than snow, and her features, which were as beautiful as a painting. Qianlong nodded. "It looks good."

Jiang Rao laughed happily and ran off to pick a few more branches of golden osmanthus, saying she wanted to take them back to the inn to put in a vase.

The two strolled through the osmanthus grove, the air thick with fragrance, the time quiet and peaceful. Walking deep into the grove, they suddenly saw a small pavilion with a stone table and stools, and a chessboard set up on the table.

"Someone was playing chess here." Jiang Rao walked over curiously and looked at the unfinished game. "Oh, this game is halfway through; why did they stop?"

Qianlong also walked over, watched for a moment, and suddenly said, "The white pieces won."

"Really?" Jiang Rao didn't understand chess and blinked at him. "How does Your Majesty know?"

Qianlong pointed at the board and explained a few things. Jiang Rao listened, only half-understanding, but still looked at him with admiration. "Your Majesty is truly amazing; you know everything."

Qianlong chuckled. "It’s just chess, nothing amazing about that."

"It is amazing," Jiang Rao insisted, then her eyes darted around. "Your Majesty, teach me how to play chess? I want to learn too."

"Now?"

"Yes!" Jiang Rao was already sitting on the stone stool, putting the pieces back into the box one by one. "Teach me starting from the simplest things."

Seeing her enthusiasm, Qianlong sat down opposite her and began to teach her. From the rules of the board to basic moves, Jiang Rao learned earnestly, though she occasionally asked questions that left him both amused and exasperated.

"Why does the Knight have to move in an 'L' shape? Can't it move in a straight line?"

"Why can't the Elephant cross the river? Can't it swim?"

"Why can the Pawn only move forward? Doesn't it want to go home?"

Qianlong was both annoyed and amused by her questions, but he explained them patiently. After teaching for about an hour, Jiang Rao finally remembered the basic rules, and the two set up the pieces for a game.

The result was, naturally, without suspense—Jiang Rao was thoroughly defeated by Qianlong. She stared at the few remaining pieces of hers on the board and pouted, "Your Majesty didn't even let me win."

"Playing chess is like commanding an army; there is no reason to let the opponent win." Qianlong smiled as he collected the pieces. "But for a beginner, you’ve done quite well."

"Really?" Jiang Rao’s eyes lit up.

"Naturally, it is true."

Jiang Rao was happy again and pestered Qianlong for another game. In this game, she had a bit more strategy; although she still lost, she lasted much longer.

The two played three games in the pavilion as the sun gradually slanted westward. The scent of osmanthus grew even richer, and the grove was quiet, save for the crisp sound of chess pieces hitting the board.

When the third game ended, Jiang Rao suddenly said, "Your Majesty, when we return to the palace, will you still teach me how to play chess?"

"If you want to learn, I will teach you," Qianlong said warmly.

"That’s a promise." Jiang Rao held out her hand. "Pinky swear."

Qianlong looked at her extended little finger and laughed. "How old are you? You still believe in this?"

"No matter how old I am, I still believe in it." Jiang Rao insisted. "Once we pinky swear, you can't go back on your word."

Qianlong sighed helplessly and hooked his little finger with hers. Jiang Rao was satisfied and began to tidy up the chess pieces.

Just then, Xiaoyanzi’s voice came from outside the grove: "My Lady! My Lord! So you're here!"

Turning to look, Xiaoyanzi, Yongqi, Ziwei, and Erkang had all arrived. Xiaoyanzi was carrying a bamboo basket and ran over excitedly. "We’ve been looking for you for so long! The innkeeper said you came to see the osmanthus, so we found you."

"Are you looking for us for something?" Jiang Rao asked.

"There’s a fireworks display in town tonight!" Xiaoyanzi’s eyes shone. "I heard it’s beautiful! Shall we go watch it together?"

"A fireworks display?" Jiang Rao became interested. "Where?"

"By the river at the east end of town," Yongqi added. "I heard it’s in preparation for tomorrow’s festival. We’ve arrived just in time."

Qianlong looked at Jiang Rao. "Do you want to go?"

"Yes!" Jiang Rao nodded, then remembered something. "But will there be a lot of people? Will it be safe?"

Erkang said, "I have already made arrangements. There is a teahouse by the river, and the private room on the second floor faces the river; the view is good, and it is quiet."

Qianlong then nodded. "Then let’s go."

The group returned to the inn for a simple dinner, and as it grew dark, they headed to the east end of town. Sure enough, the riverbank was already packed with people, with families bringing the old and the young, all waiting to see the fireworks. The private room on the second floor of the teahouse was indeed in an excellent location; pushing open the window, the entire river surface was in full view.

Jiang Rao leaned against the window, watching the bustling crowd below, and suddenly said, "It’s so lively. When we set off fireworks in the palace, although it’s grand, it always feels like there’s a barrier. It’s not like here, where the fireworks are for the common people, and everyone is truly happy."

Qianlong stood beside her and looked at her upon hearing this. "You like it this way?"

"I do." Jiang Rao turned to look at him, the lights from outside reflecting in her eyes. "It feels like the warmth of the human world."

As she spoke, a "whoosh" suddenly came from the opposite bank, and a bright light shot into the sky, blooming into a giant golden chrysanthemum in the night sky. Immediately after, countless fireworks rose into the air one after another—red, green, blue, purple... decorating the night sky in a dazzling display.

"Wow!" Xiaoyanzi was the first to exclaim, clinging to the window, unable to take her eyes off it.

Ziwei also sighed softly, "Truly beautiful."

Jiang Rao looked up, the fireworks flickering in her eyes. She suddenly felt that the brilliance of this moment was very much like life—short-lived, but extremely beautiful.

Qianlong’s arm came around from behind, gently pulling her close. Jiang Rao leaned into his embrace, and the two watched the fireworks filling the sky in silence.

Over the course of a stick of incense, hundreds of fireworks were set off, ending with a pattern of "The Dragon and Phoenix Bringing Prosperity"—a giant golden dragon and a colorful phoenix intertwined and danced in the sky, lingering for a long time and drawing cheers from the entire riverbank.

As the fireworks display ended, the crowd gradually dispersed. The group sat in the teahouse for a while longer, waiting for the crowd below to thin out before leaving.

On the way back to the inn, Jiang Rao was still immersed in the brilliance she had just witnessed. Suddenly, she asked, "Your Majesty, do you think fireworks are like life?"

"How so?"

"They are so beautiful and so bright, yet they vanish in the blink of an eye," Jiang Rao said softly. "So, one must cherish every moment of watching the fireworks, right?"

Qianlong tightened his grip on her hand. "Right."

Upon returning to the inn, they went to their respective rooms. After washing up, Jiang Rao sat at her vanity to remove her makeup, while Qianlong changed behind the screen. The candlelight flickered, and the room felt quiet and cozy.

Jiang Rao took the silver osmanthus sprig from her hair; the flowers had wilted slightly, but their fragrance remained. She carefully tucked the sprig into a book, intending to turn it into a bookmark.

Qianlong walked over and watched her through the mirror. "Are you happy today?"

"Happy." Jiang Rao turned to look at him, her eyes full of smiles. "Looking at the osmanthus, playing chess, watching the fireworks... I am happy with it all."

"That is good." Qianlong took the comb from her hand and began to brush her long hair.

Jiang Rao watched his focused expression in the mirror and suddenly asked, "Your Majesty, after we return to the palace, can we still be like this?"

"Like what?"

"Just like this," Jiang Rao said softly. "Taking walks together, playing chess together, watching the scenery together... like an ordinary married couple."

Qianlong’s hand paused. After a moment of silence, he replied, "I will try my best."

Jiang Rao knew this was the weightiest promise an emperor could give, so she asked no more. She simply turned and hugged his waist. "Your Majesty is truly kind to me."

Qianlong set down the comb and pulled her into his arms. "If I am not kind to you, to whom should I be kind?"

Jiang Rao closed her eyes in Qianlong’s embrace, her heart filled with peace.

This was good enough. At this very moment, having him by her side was the most—

chapters.title: Like a Little Child
chapters.content:
After resting for another day in Longfeng Town, the group had intended to set off the next morning, but a drizzling autumn rain began that night and had not stopped by dawn. Rain tapped against the inn’s window lattices; the streets outside were wet, yet there were still many pedestrians.

"It looks like this rain won't stop for a while," Qianlong said, standing by the window and gazing at the misty curtain of rain outside. "I fear we shall be delayed another day."

Jiang Rao had just woken up and was sitting on the bed wrapped in her quilt, her hair slightly disheveled from sleep. She rubbed her eyes, her voice still heavy with drowsiness. "Why does it always have to rain? Since it’s like this, let’s just stay one more day... Longfeng Town is quite fun anyway." As she spoke, she suddenly remembered something, and her eyes brightened. "Oh, right, Your Majesty! Didn't the innkeeper say there was a fair in town today? A fair on a rainy day?"

Qianlong turned back, sat on the edge of the bed, and reached out to smooth her messy hair. "The innkeeper said the Longfeng Town fair goes on rain or shine. They say it’s fitting to pray for favorable weather during the rain."

"Then let’s go and see!" Jiang Rao was invigorated and threw off the quilt to get out of bed, but Qianlong pressed her back down.

"What’s the rush? The rain is still heavy; let’s go when it lets up a bit." Qianlong tucked her back into the quilt. "Sleep a little longer. We walked all day yesterday—aren't you tired?"

Jiang Rao blinked and suddenly reached out to grab Qianlong’s sleeve. "Then will Your Majesty lie down with me for a while?"

Her coquettish manner softened Qianlong’s heart, and he truly took off his outer robe and lay down beside her. Jiang Rao immediately snuggled up to him like a little kitten, burrowing into his arms and finding a comfortable spot, sighing with satisfaction.

"Like a little child," Qianlong chuckled, holding her close.

"In front of Your Majesty, I will always be a little child," Jiang Rao said with righteous confidence, tracing circles on his chest with her finger. "Your Majesty must dote on me, spoil me, and accompany me."

Qianlong took hold of her mischievous hand. "Am I not doting on you enough?"

"You dote on me, but you could dote on me even more." Jiang Rao looked up, her eyes sparkling as she gazed at him. "For example, at the fair today, Your Majesty must buy me delicious things, fun things, and beautiful things..."

"Fine, fine, fine, I will buy it all." Qianlong was amused by her. "Whatever you want, I will buy."

The two chatted and laughed for a while longer. The rain outside actually began to ease, so they got up to wash and dress. After breakfast, the rain had almost stopped, and the group headed toward the fair.

The fair was held in the square at the center of town, where a high stage had already been erected. A crowd three layers deep surrounded it. A row of red silk and colorful balls hung from the stage, swaying gently in the autumn breeze.

A white-haired elder stood on the stage and announced in a clear voice, "Fellow villagers! Today is the Golden Autumn Fair, and the rules remain the same—any unmarried man or woman under the age of twenty-five may come up to compete. Whether it be zither, chess, calligraphy, painting, poetry, literature, martial arts, or acrobatics, anything goes. The villagers will judge the top three, and prizes will be awarded!"

The crowd erupted in cheers. Xiaoyanzi excitedly pulled on Yongqi. "Yongqi, you go up! Your martial arts are good; you’ll definitely win!"

Yongqi hurriedly shook his head. "This is for the local youth of the town; why should we outsiders join in the fun?"

"That’s such a pity!" Xiaoyanzi grumbled.

By then, someone had already gone up. It was a youth of sixteen or seventeen who performed a set of fist techniques. Though not exquisite, they were vigorous and spirited, winning a round of applause. Next, a young woman went up and played a piece on the pipa; the music was melodious, drawing cheers from the crowd.

Jiang Rao watched from below and suddenly tugged on Qianlong’s sleeve. "Your Majesty, look at that youth in blue; he is going to write."

Sure enough, a youth who looked like a frail scholar walked onto the stage, spread out rice paper, and picked up a brush. Before long, a piece of running-script calligraphy was finished; the characters were elegant and the brushwork powerful. The elder held it up for display, and the scholars in the crowd clicked their tongues in praise.

"The calligraphy is indeed quite good," Qianlong nodded. "It has a bit of the 'Yan tendons and Liu bones' style."

Jiang Rao tilted her head to look and whispered, "It’s still worse than Your Majesty’s calligraphy."

Qianlong laughed. "I review memorials every day and write so many words. For a youth like him, it is no small feat to write like this."

While they were talking, the performer on stage changed. This time it was a girl in red performing paper-cutting. She held a pair of scissors, and the red paper danced and turned in her hands. In just a moment, a "Dragon and Phoenix Bringing Prosperity" paper-cut was finished. The dragon and phoenix were lifelike, with even the scales and feathers detailed to the finest degree.

"Great skill!" the crowd below cheered in unison.

Xiaoyanzi felt an itch to join in and poked Yongqi. "Look how amazing that girl is! How about... I go up and perform something too?"

"You?" Yongqi raised an eyebrow. "Perform what? Climbing trees or doing somersaults?"

Xiaoyanzi glared at him, puffed up with anger. "I can do other things! I can kick a shuttlecock and I can box!"

"Then go ahead," Yongqi laughed. "I’ll be here cheering for you."

Xiaoyanzi hesitated, but in the end, she didn't go up—though she was lively, she was still a bit shy about performing in front of such a large crowd.

Just then, the stage suddenly went quiet. A youth in white slowly walked onto the stage, holding a jade flute. He bowed to the crowd, then closed his eyes to focus and brought the flute to his lips.

The flute music began, clear and melodious. At first, it was like a flowing spring, then like an autumn breeze through a forest, and finally, it seemed as if a phoenix were singing in harmony, spiraling upward. The entire venue fell silent; everyone was immersed in the sound of the flute.

Jiang Rao listened, mesmerized, and said softly, "This flute is played so beautifully..."

Qianlong also nodded. "Rare indeed. This youth is only eighteen or nineteen, yet his flute skills have reached a state of perfection."

As the piece ended, the lingering notes seemed to echo in the rafters. After a long moment, thunderous applause erupted from the crowd. The youth in white bowed in thanks, his expression calm, possessing a demeanor of being unmoved by favor or humiliation.

Several others performed afterward, but none were as brilliant as the youth in white. When the final judging took place, the youth in white won first place without any suspense, the paper-cutting girl took second, and the scholarly youth took third.

The elder presented the prizes—a pair of dragon and phoenix jade pendants, a gold hairpin, and an inkstone—to the three. The youth in white accepted the pendants but said, "I offered my performance only to make friends through music; I dare not accept such a generous gift. These pendants... please pass them on to the person among today’s contestants who is most in need of help."

The crowd began to buzz with discussion. The elder pondered for a moment and said, "Very well, it shall be done as you say." He looked at the crowd. "Among today’s contestants, is there anyone from a difficult family background who needs help?"

A thin, frail youth timidly raised his hand. "I... my mother is ill, and I have no money to buy medicine..."

The elder nodded and handed the jade pendants to the youth. "Take them and go treat your mother."

The youth took the pendants, tears streaming down his face, and kowtowed in thanks repeatedly.

Watching this scene, Jiang Rao said softly, "This youth in white is truly kind-hearted."

Qianlong also nodded. "Virtuous and talented; a rare find."

The fair ended, and the crowd gradually dispersed. Everyone prepared to return to the inn to collect their luggage and set off. Just as they were about to leave, the youth in white suddenly walked over and bowed to Qianlong and the others. "You are not from around here, are you?"

Qianlong returned the bow. "Just passing through, and stopped to join the fun."

The youth smiled. "Just now, while watching from the stage, I noticed your extraordinary bearing, especially this gentleman," he said, looking at Qianlong. "Your eyes are wise; you must not be an ordinary merchant. If I may be so bold, may I ask for your honorable name?"

Qianlong remained composed. "My surname is Ai, from the capital. Little brother, your flute skills are superb; I am truly impressed."

"I dare not accept such praise," the youth said modestly. "My surname is Bai, and my given name is Yu. I have loved the flute since childhood and have only achieved a little success." He paused. "Are you all leaving now?"

"Indeed."

A flash of regret crossed Bai Yu’s eyes. "That is truly a pity. I had originally hoped to invite you to my home for a chat and to seek your guidance."

Jiang Rao suddenly asked, "The phoenix singing in harmony in your flute music—did you conceive that yourself?"

Bai Yu looked at her, surprise flashing in his eyes. "The lady noticed? It is indeed my own creation. My mother once said that the value of flute music lies in the intent; without intent, even the most skillful technique is nothing but craftsmanship."

"Your mother has profound insights," Qianlong praised.

Bai Yu smiled. "My mother was also a music lover in her youth, but unfortunately, her health is poor now, and she cannot hear the flute in person." He sighed, then brightened again. "If you are not in a hurry, why not come to my humble home for a cup of tea? If my mother knew that a kindred spirit had visited, she would be very happy."

Qianlong and Jiang Rao exchanged a look. Jiang Rao said softly, "Your Majesty, it is still early..."

Qianlong nodded. "Then we shall impose upon you."

Bai Yu’s home was at the southern end of town, a quiet little courtyard. A few clusters of green bamboo were planted in the yard, and the wind rustling through the leaves created a very elegant atmosphere. Bai’s mother was a woman in her forties; though she looked ill, her temperament was gentle. Hearing that guests had arrived, she hurriedly had her maid prepare tea.

The group sat in a bamboo pavilion. Bai’s mother poured the tea herself and smiled. "My home is humble; please forgive the lack of refinement."

"You are too kind, Madam," Qianlong said, taking the teacup. "This courtyard is quiet and elegant; it is a wonderful place."

Bai’s mother looked at Qianlong for a moment, then suddenly said, "Your bearing is extraordinary, sir; it reminds me of an old friend."

Qianlong raised an eyebrow. "Oh? And which old friend might that be?"

Mother Bai shook her head with a faint smile: "That was many years ago; it is not worth mentioning." She turned to look at Jiang Rao: "The embroidery on your dress, Madam, is exquisite. Is it Su embroidery?"

Jiang Rao was wearing a water-green qipao today, with intertwined lotus patterns embroidered on the cuffs and collar; it was indeed Su embroidery. She nodded: "You have a sharp eye, Madam."

"I also loved embroidery when I was young," Mother Bai said, a look of nostalgia appearing in her eyes. "The splitting of threads in Su embroidery is fine and dense, and the stitches are even; it is the ultimate test of skill. The embroiderer who made your dress must be a master."

The two women began to chat about embroidery and found they had much in common. Although Mother Bai was frail, her conversation revealed a high level of learning and cultivation, unlike that of an ordinary woman.

On the other side, Bai Yu brought out a jade flute and played another piece. This melody was gentle and soothing, like a spring breeze brushing against one's face. Jiang Rao listened intently, and only after the music ended did she say: "Young Master Bai, was this piece composed for your mother?"

Bai Yu nodded: "My mother has been lonely during her illness, so I composed this 'Spring Radiance Melody,' hoping she would feel as if bathed in a spring breeze and recover soon."

"A commendable display of filial piety," Qianlong praised.

The group stayed at the Bai residence for over an hour, conversing happily. As they were leaving, Mother Bai had Bai Yu bring out a brocade box and handed it to Jiang Rao: "Meeting you felt like reuniting with an old friend. Please accept this small token as a gesture of my sincerity."

Jiang Rao opened the box to find a pair of delicate embroidered sachets. They were embroidered with twin lotus flowers on a single stalk, with fine, dense stitches and elegant colors.

"I embroidered these when I was young. Now that my eyesight is failing, I can no longer embroider like this," Mother Bai said with a smile. "I give them to you, Madam, wishing you and your husband a lifetime of harmony."

Jiang Rao was both surprised and delighted, and she thanked her earnestly. Qianlong also had Ji Xiaolan bring out a pair of mutton-fat jade bracelets to gift to Mother Bai for her health.

It was nearly noon when they left the Bai residence. The group returned to the inn to collect their luggage and finally set off.

In the carriage, Jiang Rao held the pair of sachets, unable to put them down. Qianlong smiled: "You like them that much?"

"Mm," Jiang Rao nodded. "Mother Bai's embroidery is truly wonderful, and... she is genuinely wishing us well." She tied the sachets to her own waist and Qianlong's, one on each side, making a perfect pair.

Qianlong looked at the swaying sachets at their waists and shook his head with a laugh: "You, you just love these things."

"It’s the sentiment that counts," Jiang Rao said, leaning on his shoulder. "Don't you think so, Your Majesty? The people we've met on this incognito tour have all been so interesting. The waist drums of Plum Blossom Town, the marriage tree of Matchmaker Town, the spiritual spring of Ling Mountain Town, the festival in Dragon-Phoenix Town, and refined people like Mother Bai... these are things one never sees in the palace."

Qianlong took her hand: "That is why I brought you out to see. To see my empire and my subjects."

Jiang Rao looked up at him: "Then will you bring me out again in the future?"

"I will," Qianlong said warmly. "I will bring you out for a trip every year."

Jiang Rao smiled, feeling completely satisfied.
